Losing this node's stake makes the left red box vulnerable as π<sup>s</sup> = 2σ<sup>v</sup> when s is a red box, which is represented when one goes from the upper right box to the middle right box in attack (A<sup>1</sup> , B<sup>1</sup> ). This attack now leads the middle red service vulnerable and it is attacked in (A<sup>3</sup> , B<sup>3</sup> ). We consider f(π, A) = P s∈A π<sup>s</sup> as the profit function. Note that each individual service cannot be attacked here as π<sup>i</sup> < σ<sup>i</sup> for i ∈ {1, 2}. However, the set S might be vulnerable since the profitability condition \(1\), π<sup>1</sup> + π<sup>2</sup> > σ<sup>i</sup> holds for the potential attack ({s<sup>1</sup> , s2}, {vi}) ⊂ S × V . This attack is only valid, however, if σ<sup>i</sup> > αs<sup>j</sup> (σ<sup>1</sup> + σ<sup>2</sup> ), which implies that we need to have <sup>α</sup>s<sup>j</sup> <sup>&</sup>lt; <sup>1</sup> 2 for j ∈ {1, 2} for this to be an attack. So if s<sup>1</sup> , s<sup>2</sup> were BFT protocols with α<sup>s</sup> = 1 3 , this graph would be insecure. However, if it they were longest-chain protocols with α<sup>s</sup> = 1 2 , it would be secure.

usages.alt: Figure 1 of the paper: a restaking graph of two services and two operators
usages.caption: Figure 1 of the paper: two services (orange) are each secured by the same two operators (blue). Corrupting either service is worth 1, and each operator stakes 1.1, so attacking one service alone loses more than it gains. Because one operator's stake secures both services, attacking both at once gains 2 for a loss of 1.1 under the additive profit of earlier work.
